title: Other Software
text:
In addition to R packages, in an earlier life, I developed extensive collections of SAS software for statistical graphics and data analysis.








NoteMaintenance Status



These macros are no longer actively maintained but remain available as a historical resource and for those still using SAS.


I have developed an extensive collection of SAS macros for statistical graphics and data analysis. These macros cover a wide range of statistical methods with an emphasis on graphical display.



Graphical methods: Scatterplot matrices, enhanced plots, diagnostic displays
Multivariate methods: Correspondence analysis, canonical correlation, discriminant analysis
Categorical data: Mosaic displays, odds ratio plots, loglinear models
Regression diagnostics: Influence plots, partial regression plots
Statistical graphics: Quantile plots, rootograms, and more








Documentation
Comprehensive documentation for each macro with examples and usage notes.
Browse documentation →






Source Code
All macro source code is freely available on GitHub.
View on GitHub →








Additional software tools and utilities are available through my GitHub repositories at github.com/friendly.

title: Welcome to My Site
text:
I’m a Professor of Psychology at York University, specializing in data visualization and statistical methods. My research focuses on development of graphical methods for understanding multivariate data and models and visualization for categorical data. Another passion is the study of the history of data visualization, captured in my Milestones Project and historical research papers.
More about me →




Scan to visit










I maintain over 15 R packages for multivariate analysis, categorical data analysis, and historical datasets. These packages emphasize visualization and understanding of statistical methods.
Explore packages →



Author of several books on data visualization and statistical methods in R, including works on visualizing multivariate models and discrete data analysis.

title: Books
text:
I have authored and co-authored several books on data visualization and statistical methods in R. These books emphasize graphical understanding of statistical concepts and practical implementation.






A comprehensive guide to understanding multivariate linear models through visualization. Covers HE plots, canonical discriminant analysis, and other graphical methods for multivariate data.
Status: Under review. To be published by CRC Press, 2026. Available online
Read online →










Co-authored with David Meyer, this book provides an accessible introduction to the major methods of categorical data analysis for data exploration, statistical testing and visualization. As opposed to more theoretical books, the goal here is to help the reader to translate theory into practical application, by providing skills and software tools for carrying out these methods.
Publication information: Michael Friendly and David Meyer, Discrete Data Analysis with R: Visualization and Modeling Techniques for Categorical and Count Data, 2016, Chapman and Hall/CRC, ISBN 9781498725835.
Book website →










Co-authored with Howard Wainer, this book provides a comprehensive historical account of data visualization. It addresses three central questions: How did graphic representations of numerical data originate and why? What innovations led to the common graphs and diagrams we use today? How have graphical inventions contributed to understanding phenomena and communicating findings?
Publication information: Michael Friendly and Howard Wainer, A History of Data Visualization & Graphic Communication, 2021, Harvard University Press, ISBN 978-0674975231.
Companion website →






For more information about my books and related materials, visit my books page at datavis.ca.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text: Six Palmer penguins, wearing their names at last. Each is drawn to caricature what makes it unusual: Cyrano’s long bill, Snub Nose’s short, deep one (call him Socrates, after history’s most famous snub nose), Falstaff’s girth, Tinkerbell’s slight build, the BFG’s long flippers, and Average Joe, who is just a big Gentoo. Image generated by ChatGPT, from the author’s description of the six birds and their measurements; see About the banner at the end.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Overheard at Biscoe Point


“Hey Bro, have you noticed? All these scientists measured us up the wazoo, published papers, and now our data is famous. They use us to teach statistics and data graphics all over the world. But sadly, they don’t even know our names, even with those tags on our flippers.”
“And why didn’t they bother to give us the Big Five personality scales? Those orange Adélies are often narcissistic extroverts, not very open to experience. I’m a proud, average Joe Gentoo. Let’s teach them a thing or two.”

They have a point. It’s also an interesting data-analysis challenge. The Palmer penguins are identified only by numbers: their row numbers in a data frame. Even those aren’t stable. They depend on whether the few birds with missing measurements were dropped: Cyrano, whom you’ll meet shortly, is number 294 in palmerpenguins::penguins and number 283 in heplots::peng. The original data, palmerpenguins::penguins_raw, does record an Individual ID for each bird (Cyrano is N71A2), but those codes are recycled: the 344 birds share just 190 of them. And they were dropped from the simplified data frames everyone uses, so our penguin friends never got rownames().
T. S. Eliot warned that “The Naming of Cats is a difficult matter,” because a cat must have three different names. Penguins have the same problem. Cyrano’s everyday name is a row number, 283 or 294, depending on which data frame you ask. Her more particular name, the one for the field notebook, is N71A2, which she shares with other birds. And then there is the third name, “the name that no human research can discover.” Eliot says the cat “himself knows, and will never confess.” Cyrano knows hers too. Our nicknames are only a guess at it.

Sorry
This post can stand as a public apology from the R community. It’s my attempt to right this injustice to the 344 birds on Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen islands near Palmer Station who allowed themselves to be measured for science from 2007 to 2009.

Hey, guys: I understand your pain. I hope you don’t mind my human, literary, historical references I’ve used to give you names.


As it turns out, a few of them do have names. Cara Thompson named four: Cyrano, the BFG, Tinkerbell and Average Joe. I borrowed Cyrano for my book, and added a Hook Nose of my own. This post renames him, and names one more. So the questions for this post are: what makes each of these birds unusual, and do their names fit?

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Naming names


Data and the named birds used here
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

data(peng, package = "heplots")    # palmerpenguins, 333 complete cases

col <- c("Adélie" = "#F37A00", Chinstrap = "#6A3D9A", Gentoo = "#33a02c")

# the named birds, by row number in heplots::peng
named <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~name,         ~namer,
  283, "Cyrano",       "Thompson",
  124, "The BFG",      "Thompson",
  304, "Tinkerbell",   "Thompson",
  166, "Average Joe",  "Thompson",
   10, "Snub Nose",    "Friendly",
   35, "Falstaff",     "Friendly"
)

peng <- peng |>
  mutate(id         = row_number(),
         species    = factor(species, labels = c("Adélie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo")),
         bill_shape = log(bill_length) - log(bill_depth),
         stoutness  = log(body_mass) / 3 - log(flipper_length)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(z_shape = c(scale(bill_shape)),
         z_stout = c(scale(stoutness))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(named, by = "id") |>
  mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(name), NA, paste0(name, " (", id, ")")))
birds <- filter(peng, !is.na(name))


I first got to know the Palmer penguins when I found that they made good examples for methods of multivariate data visualization. I adopted them as a running example in my book, Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R, where they turn up in nearly every chapter.

Three noteworthy birds
In Chapter 4, I went looking for multivariate outliers. As in the Bob Marley song, I found “three little birds, pitch by my doorstep.” As I hope to say to my Palmer friends, “Don’t worry about a thing, ’cause every little thing gonna be all right.”
The first tool I usually use to identify possible outliers in multivariate data is a heplots::cqplot(), which shows the squared Mahalanobis distance, \(D^2\), of each bird from the centroid of all four measures (bill length and depth, flipper length, body mass), taking their variances and correlations into account, plotted against their \(\chi^2\) quantiles in a multivariate normal distribution.
Three birds came out on top: cases 283, 10 and 35. The chi-square QQ plot showed that only one of them, 283, falls outside the 95% envelope. The other two are just the most unusual of an ordinary lot.


Code
library(heplots)
vars <- c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "flipper_length", "body_mass")
DSQ <- Mahalanobis(peng[, vars])

cqplot(peng[, vars],
       id.n = 3,
       col = col[peng$species],
       pch = c(19, 17, 15)[peng$species],
       ref.col = "grey",
       what = "Penguin numeric variables",
       cex.lab = 1.25)








Figure 1: Chi-square QQ plot of the penguins’ squared Mahalanobis distances on the four measures, with a 95% confidence envelope. Only case 283 lies outside it.





Plotting bill length against bill depth with those three labeled, two of them looked odd for their species. Case 283, a Chinstrap, has a remarkably long bill, so I called her “Cyrano”, after the long-nosed hero of Edmond Rostand’s play. Case 10, an Adélie with a short, deep bill, became “Hook Nose”. Case 35 looked unremarkable in that view and stayed nameless until today.


Code
three <- order(DSQ, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
peng_plot <- peng |> mutate(note = id %in% three)

ggplot(peng_plot,
       aes(x = bill_length, y = bill_depth,
           colour = species, shape = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = note), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(1.5, 4)) +
  geom_text(data = subset(peng_plot, note),
            aes(label = id), fontface = "bold",
            nudge_y = .4, colour = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.95, alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.15))








Figure 2: Bill length against bill depth, with 95% data ellipses and regression lines for each species. The three birds with the largest \(D^2\) are labeled.





The names stuck, at least for me. Cyrano reappears throughout the book: dancing around the edges of a grand tour, at the extreme ends of a biplot, as the most influential case in a multivariate linear model, and finally getting a weight of zero in a robust fit. Using heplots::robmlm() I could just say, “Bye-bye Cyrano—it’s been fun—but we can get along nicely without you.” That is the point of a name: a reader can follow Cyrano from chapter to chapter in a way they can’t follow “case 283”.


Where “Cyrano” came from
I thought I had made up the name. It turns out I hadn’t. I’d seen it in Cara Thompson’s poster for useR! 2022, Level Up Your Labels: Tips and Tricks for Annotating Plots, filed it away, and forgotten where it came from. My code for the book still had a comment, # From Cara Thompson, above her lines that picked out the birds (with her name misspelled, which didn’t help).
Her poster image is a wonderful lesson in plot annotation. Its plot, titled “Perfectly proportional penguins—with a few exceptions!”, shows flipper length against bill length, and replaces a legend and a lot of explanation with a few well-placed text boxes. Four birds get names and a sentence each:

The BFG: “Sitting comfortably within the cluster of Gentoos, this Adelie penguin defies the predictions of his species on both flipper length and bill length.”
Tinkerbell: “The smallest penguin in the set defies the odds on weight for her species and flipper and bill length.”
Average Joes: “The Gentoos tend to stick to their trend, with very few outliers. Heavier penguins have longer flippers and longer bills.”
Cyrano: “With an exceptionally long bill and the shortest flippers bar one among the Chinstraps, this little guy is sure to stand out!”







Figure 3: Cara Thompson’s plot from her useR! 2022 poster, Level Up Your Labels. © Cara Thompson, reused under CC BY 4.0.



Did she really pick these birds by eye, from one plot? As we’ll see, every one of her descriptions holds up, except perhaps “little guy”: Cyrano is a female.


Who gets a label?
Thompson’s poster had a second effect on me. In her plot, and in mine in the book, the labeled birds were chosen by hand, and the labels were added by a small piece of ggplot2 plumbing: compute something, make a logical variable for the cases to label, then add a geom_text() layer for just those rows. It works, but you have to do it again for every plot.
Base R graphics handle this better than ggplot2, thanks to the car package. Nearly every plotting function in car takes an argument like id = list(n = 3, method = "mahal"), and labels the 3 points furthest from the centroid, with no further work. The method can be "x", "y", "r" for residuals, or a vector such as Cook’s distances. Labeling unusual points becomes a decision about which criterion, not a chore.
I pulled that selection logic out into a function, heplots::noteworthy(), which takes x, y, n and a method, and returns the row numbers of the points to label. The criterion needn’t come from the two variables on the axes. You can supply a computed vector of criteria values. Here it finds the book’s three birds, using \(D^2\) on all four measures, for a plot of just two:


Code
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 3, method = DSQ)


#> [1] 283  10  35


That isn’t what Thompson would have found with a formula. The default, method = "mahal", on the two variables in her plot picks out a different set:


Code
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 6, method = "mahal")


#> [1] 283 179 314 272 329 297


Cyrano (283) is first again, but the rest (179, 314, 272, …) are birds on the edges of the overall cloud, which spans three species. None of the BFG, Tinkerbell or Average Joe is on that list. Her eye was doing something the formula wasn’t: judging each bird against its own species. I’ll come back to that.
The next step was to make this a ggplot2 layer, stat_noteworthy(), so that any plot could say which points to label in the same vocabulary. With help from the ggplot2 extenders club, I got a working version. Getting it generally right turned out to be harder:

With groups, should it pick the \(n\) most unusual points overall, or \(n\) in each group? The usual ggplot2 habit is per group. A statistician usually wants the most unusual points in the plot as a whole. Both are reasonable, so it should probably be an option.
With facets, the selection should be done separately in each panel.
Higher dimensions: the penguins’ case is the hardest. The criterion (\(D^2\) over four variables) lives in more dimensions than the plot shows. A ggplot2 stat sees only the variables mapped to aesthetics, so there’s no clean way to hand it the others.

So stat_noteworthy() is still in the development folder of heplots, a branch partly leafed out, waiting for another season. Meanwhile the penguins wait for their names.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
One view in 2D
To see the six birds together, Figure 4 reproduces Thompson’s plot, without her annotations: flipper length against bill length, with the size of each point showing body mass. Her four named birds and my two are labeled with their case numbers in heplots::peng.
Her four are easy to find. Cyrano is alone at the right, far beyond the other Chinstraps. The BFG is an orange point among the green Gentoos. Tinkerbell is the smallest point among the Chinstraps, and Average Joe sits in the middle of the Gentoos. But Snub Nose and Falstaff don’t stand out. Snub Nose is at the short-bill edge of the Adélies, but not beyond it, and Falstaff is lost in the crowd. What makes them unusual will need another view.


Code
ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length, flipper_length, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = body_mass), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = birds, aes(size = body_mass), shape = 21,
             colour = "black", stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_size(range = c(0.5, 7), breaks = c(3000, 4500, 6000),
             labels = \(x) paste(x / 1000, "kg")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species", size = "Body mass") +
  guides(size = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "grey50")),
         colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.02, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1), legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))








Figure 4: Thompson’s view of the penguins: flipper length against bill length, with point size showing body mass. Her four named birds are joined by two more from my book.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
What makes a penguin unusual?
To say why a bird is unusual, you need a better question than “which of its four measures is extreme?” A long bill is only part of a description: is it also deep, or unusually slender? And a heavy penguin may just be a big penguin. The two earlier posts in this series took up exactly these questions, by re-expressing the four measures as variables that mean something:

In Thinking about Penguin Variables, bill length (\(L\)) and depth (\(D\)) became bill size, \(\log L + \log D\), and bill shape, \(\log (L / D)\): is the bill long and slender, or short and stubby?
In Penguin Bodies, flipper length (\(F\)) and body mass (\(M\)) became body size, \(\log F + \log M / 3\), and stoutness, \(\log (M^{1/3} / F)\): is the bird heavy or light for its flipper length? Cubed, this is \(M / F^3\), a penguin version of the condition factor used for fish.

Within species, these four are nearly uncorrelated, except that bigger birds have bigger bills (bill size with body size, \(r = 0.70\)). The two size variables mostly say what you’d expect: big birds are big all over.1 What gives a bird its character is its proportions, and those are what the names are about: a long nose, a snub nose, a stout body, a slight one. So here I use just the two ratios, bill shape and stoutness. Bill shape is dimensionless; stoutness, as \(M / F^3\), has units of density, but standardizing within species makes both free of units. The two are almost exactly uncorrelated within species (\(r = -0.03\)).

Compared with whom?
The second, and more important, question for doing right by our penguin friends is: unusual compared with whom? What are the aspects of their measurements that we should take into account (control or adjust for) in declaring a bird name-worthy?
Cyrano’s bill, at 3.26 times as long as it is deep, would be unremarkable on a Gentoo, whose bills average 3.18. On a Chinstrap, it is the most slender bill by a wide margin. A Gentoo’s bill on a Gentoo isn’t news; on a Chinstrap it is.
So I standardize each variable within species: a bird’s \(z\)-score is its distance from its own species’ mean, in units of that species’ standard deviation. This also puts the species on a common scale, which matters because they don’t vary equally: Adélie bills vary more in shape than the others. Males and females are pooled. Males are bigger, but on these two ratios the sexes differ little, except that Adélie males are a bit stouter.
This is where Cara Thompson’s eye and the book’s formula parted company. The book’s \(D^2\) measured each bird’s distance from the centroid of all the penguins, ignoring species. By that measure the BFG ranks 89th of 333: a large Adélie sits comfortably inside the overall cloud, close to the Gentoos. Judged against other Adélies, with the same \(D^2\) computed within species, he is the third most unusual bird in the data. Thompson saw that from one plot.
Table 1 gives the six birds’ bill ratios and stoutness indices as recorded, and their \(z\)-scores within species. The raw measurements are in the next section below.


Code
birds |>
  mutate(name   = factor(name, levels = named$name[c(1, 5, 6, 3, 2, 4)]),
         LD     = bill_length / bill_depth,
         MF3    = 1000 * body_mass / flipper_length^3) |>
  arrange(name) |>
  select(name, id, species, sex, LD, MF3, z_shape, z_stout) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Name", "Case", "Species", "Sex", "L / D", "M / F³",
                             "z shape", "z stoutness"))




Table 1: The named birds: bill length / depth and the stoutness index M / F³ (in g/cm³), as recorded, and bill shape and stoutness as z-scores within species. Species means of L / D are 2.12 (Adélie), 2.65 (Chinstrap) and 3.18 (Gentoo); of M / F³, 0.54, 0.50 and 0.50.

Figure 5 is the main event: every bird, placed by bill shape and stoutness within its species. Because the two are nearly uncorrelated and on the same scale, it reads like a map. An ordinary penguin sits near the center; the farther a bird lies from it, in any direction, the more unusual it is; and the direction says why. To the right, slender bills; to the left, stubby ones. Up is stout, down is lean.


Code
lim <- c(-4.2, 4.2)
ggplot(peng, aes(z_shape, z_stout, colour = species)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.95, colour = "grey40",
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.68, colour = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = birds, shape = 21, size = 3.5, colour = "black",
             aes(fill = species), stroke = 1.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.7, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  coord_equal(xlim = lim, ylim = lim) +
  labs(x = "← stubby    Bill shape, z within species    slender →",
       y = "← lean    Stoutness, z within species    stout →",
       colour = "Species") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.88, 0.14),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))








Figure 5: Bill shape against stoutness, as z-scores within species. The ellipses enclose about 68% and 95% of the birds. The named birds lie in contrasting directions from the center; Average Joe marks the center itself.





The named birds spread out to the edges, in pairs of opposites. Cyrano lies far to the right, the most slender bill for her species, and Snub Nose far to the left, among the stubbiest: the long nose and the short one. Falstaff is at the top and Tinkerbell at the bottom: the stoutest and the slightest. The BFG is off in the lower right, with a slender bill and a lean body, not the most extreme on either alone, but unusual on both. Average Joe sits almost exactly at the center.
Two of these birds were hard to see in Thompson’s view (Figure 4). Snub Nose’s bill is short, but no shorter than a few other Adélies’, and Falstaff’s flippers are short, but not remarkably so. What marks them out is a ratio: bill length to depth for Snub Nose, mass to flipper length for Falstaff. A plot of the raw measures can’t show a ratio unless you know to look for it.
The map also turns up birds that nobody has named yet. The stubbiest bill for its species isn’t Snub Nose’s but that of a Gentoo male, case 183 (z = −3.93, against −3.43 for Snub Nose). Snub Nose has the stubbiest bill of all 333 as measured, at 1.64, but Adélie bills are stubby to begin with. Likewise, two Gentoo males, 160 and 253, are as stout among Gentoos as Falstaff is among Adélies.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Do the names fit?
Assigning a name to a Palmer penguin from afar is a data analyst’s one-word theory of what makes a bird unusual. Here are the six, in relation to the data shown in plots, with their measurements and a verdict on each name. Means in parentheses are for birds of the same species and sex.

Cyrano (283): the long nose
Cyrano, a Chinstrap female, has the longest bill of any Chinstrap: 58.0 mm (mean 46.6). But its depth is ordinary, 17.8 mm (mean 17.6), so it is long and slender. At 3.26 times as long as it is deep, it is far beyond any other Chinstrap’s (the next is 2.93), and more slender than the average Gentoo bill. She has a Gentoo’s bill on a Chinstrap’s body. She is also stout, the second part of her story: a normal mass, 3700 g (mean 3527), on flippers of 181 mm (mean 192), among the shortest of the Chinstraps. Thompson’s label, “an exceptionally long bill and the shortest flippers bar one among the Chinstraps”, is exact.
Verdict: The name fits perfectly. Rostand’s Cyrano de Bergerac has the most famous nose in literature, the subject of a whole speech in the play: “C’est un roc! … c’est un pic! … c’est un cap! Que dis-je, c’est un cap? … C’est une péninsule!” (It’s a rock, a peak, a cape! A cape, did I say? It’s a peninsula!) That Cyrano is a female, which Thompson’s “little guy” missed, doesn’t matter. A nose like that transcends gender.


Snub Nose (“Socrates”) (10): formerly Hook Nose
Case 10, an Adélie male, has the opposite bill: short, 34.6 mm (mean 40.4), and deep, 21.1 mm (mean 19.1), at the 4th and 97th percentiles of the Adélies. Its ratio of 1.64 (mean 2.12) is the lowest of all 333 penguins; the next is 1.76. The rest of him is a large but ordinary Adélie male.
I called him “Hook Nose” in the book, describing “a very short and curved bill.” That was my mistake: bill depth is measured top to bottom at the base of the bill. It says how thick the bill is, not how curved. Nothing in the data measures a hook. What he has is a snub nose.
Verdict: “Hook Nose” doesn’t fit; Snub Nose does, and says so plainly. For those who know their history, his alias is Socrates, owner of the best documented snub nose there is. Plato and Xenophon both mention it, and in Xenophon’s Symposium Socrates argues, tongue in cheek, that it is the more beautiful kind, because upturned nostrils catch scents from every direction. Cyrano and Snub Nose make a pair, the long nose and the snub nose: one has a bill too slender for her species, the other too stubby for his. One caveat, from the map: relative to its own species, the stubbiest bill belongs to Gentoo 183, still nameless.


Falstaff (35): the stout one
Case 35, another Adélie male, has a bill that is average in every respect: 39.8 by 19.1 mm, against means of 40.4 and 19.1. It is his body that stands out. At 4650 g (mean 4043), he is one of the heaviest Adélies, 97th percentile, but his flippers are short, 184 mm (mean 192). That makes him, on the raw index M/F³ = 0.75, the stoutest penguin in the data; the next is 0.69. (Within species, two Gentoos are as extreme, relative to other Gentoos.) In the book (Chapter 5), he showed up at the edge of a biplot of the smallest principal components, where I guessed that he was “probably much heavier than most and has short flippers”. That was right, but I didn’t give him a name.
Verdict: Falstaff, Shakespeare’s fat knight in Henry IV, who pleads “banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.” He is a new name, so the only question is whether it fits. I think it does, though a fuller comparison takes some of the stuffing out of him (see Going further).


Tinkerbell (304): the slight one
Tinkerbell, a Chinstrap female, is the lightest penguin in the data: 2700 g (mean 3527); the next lightest weighs 2850 g. But she is not simply small. Her flippers, 192 mm, are exactly the average for a Chinstrap female, and her bill is an ordinary length, if shallow. She is light for her size. On M/F³ = 0.38, she is the least stout bird of all 333, and the most extreme on stoutness within species too. She is Falstaff’s mirror image: his M/F³ is 31% above the mean for Adélie males, hers 24% below the mean for Chinstrap females.
Verdict: Thompson’s label calls her “the smallest penguin in the set.” “Lightest” is more precise, since her flippers are ordinary. But Barrie’s Tinker Bell is a tiny fairy, and the name suits a bird that weighs less than she should. It fits. (Barrie did describe his Tinker Bell as “slightly inclined to embonpoint”, but we needn’t tell her.)


The BFG (124): the impostor
The BFG is an Adélie male with the longest flippers of any Adélie: 210 mm (mean 192); the next is 208. His bill is long for an Adélie, 44.1 mm (mean 40.4), but shallower, 18.0 mm (mean 19.1), so it is slender. He is not heavy: 4000 g (mean 4043). Long flippers on an ordinary mass make him lean.
In Thompson’s view, flipper length against bill length, he sits “comfortably within the cluster of Gentoos”. A discriminant analysis on just those two variables would call him a Gentoo, with a posterior probability of 0.97. On all four measures, it wouldn’t. His bill is still deep for a Gentoo. None of his oddities is extreme on its own, which is why the book’s \(D^2\), ignoring species, ranked him 89th. Taken together, against other Adélies, he is the third most unusual bird in the data.
Verdict: It fits beautifully. Dahl’s Big Friendly Giant is the gentle runt among giants, much smaller than the others. That’s the BFG here: a giant among Adélies, but a small Gentoo.


Average Joe (166): the reference bird
Thompson’s text box was for the “Average Joes”, plural: the Gentoos, who “tend to stick to their trend, with very few outliers.” The bird her arrow points to is Gentoo male 166, and he is average indeed. His flippers, 222 mm, are exactly the mean for a Gentoo male. His bill, 48.7 by 15.1 mm (means 49.5 by 15.7), and his mass, 5350 g (mean 5485), are close to it. On the map, he sits near the center (z = 0.31 and −0.17). Among all 333 birds, by \(D^2\) within species, he ranks 319th: only 14 birds are more ordinary.
Verdict: It fits, and it earns its place. Every gallery of oddities needs one ordinary specimen to show what “normal” looks like. He is the reference bird.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
What’s in a name?
Thompson’s names come from fiction: Rostand’s Cyrano, Barrie’s Tinker Bell, Dahl’s Big Friendly Giant, and the everyman. Each one describes a body, not a personality. My two join that family: Falstaff from Shakespeare, and Snub Nose, a plain description like Average Joe’s, with Socrates as his literary alias. Together they make three pairs. Cyrano and Snub Nose are the long nose and the short one; Falstaff and Tinkerbell, the stoutest and the slightest; the BFG, an Adélie who passes for a Gentoo, and Average Joe, a Gentoo who passes for nothing but himself.
There is a statistical point under the fun. A name helps us remember a point; a good choice of variables tells us why it is unusual. The book’s \(D^2\), computed on the four measures as recorded and ignoring species, found Cyrano, Snub Nose and Falstaff, but ranked the BFG 89th. Thompson’s plot of two raw measures found Cyrano, the BFG and Tinkerbell, but Snub Nose and Falstaff looked ordinary there. I misread my own plot and named a bird for a hook that nothing in the data could measure. Once the measures were re-expressed as bill shape and stoutness, and each bird was compared with its own species, every one of the six landed in a place that said what was special about it, and the names could be checked against that. Of the five names these birds had before, four hold up; Hook Nose has been retired with thanks.
That leaves birds that are just as unusual and still go by a row number. Gentoo male 183 has the stubbiest bill for his species, stubbier relative to other Gentoos than Snub Nose’s is among the Adélies. “Pug” would do, or “Puffin”, if naming a penguin after another bird isn’t an insult. Gentoo males 160 and 253 are as stout as Falstaff, relative to their species. Suggestions are welcome: by email, or wherever you found this post.
As for the penguins of Biscoe Point, a few of them can now be called by their names. The Big Five personality scales will have to wait for another field season.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Going further
The \(z\)-scores in this post are standardized residuals from a model, though I didn’t call them that: the simplest one, ~ species, applied to one variable at a time. “Compared with whom?” has a fuller answer. A penguin is not only a member of its species; it is also male or female, and it was measured in a particular year. And the four re-expressed variables are not quite independent: bill size goes with body size.
A multivariate linear model handles all of that at once. Fit the four variables, bill size and shape, body size and stoutness, to species, sex and year, and take each bird’s Mahalanobis \(D^2\) from its residuals, using their pooled covariance. Then a bird is unusual relative to birds of the same species and sex, measured in the same year, with the correlations among the variables taken into account. Including year deals with something found in Penguin Bodies: flippers measured in 2007 were shorter, in all three species, most likely because of how they were measured.


Residual D² from a sequence of models
peng <- peng |>
  mutate(bill_size = log(bill_length) + log(bill_depth),
         body_size = log(flipper_length) + log(body_mass) / 3,
         fyear     = factor(year))

models <- c("Ignoring species" = "1",
            "Species"          = "species",
            "+ sex"            = "species * sex",
            "+ year"           = "species * sex + fyear")

resid_D2 <- function(rhs) {
  fit <- lm(reformulate(rhs, "cbind(bill_size, bill_shape, body_size, stoutness)"), data = peng)
  R <- resid(fit)
  mahalanobis(R, center = 0, cov = crossprod(R) / fit$df.residual)
}

ranks <- sapply(models, \(rhs) rank(-resid_D2(rhs)))


Figure 6 follows the named birds as the comparison group is refined, from the whole colony to birds of the same species, sex and year.


Code
rank_long <- as.data.frame(ranks[birds$id, ]) |>
  mutate(name = birds$name, species = birds$species) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(name, species), names_to = "model", values_to = "rank") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(models)))

ggplot(rank_long, aes(model, rank, group = name, colour = species)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = subset(rank_long, model == "+ year"),
            aes(label = paste0(name, " (", rank, ")")),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.08, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = c("log10", "reverse"),
                     breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 333)) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.3, 1.3))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  labs(x = "Model for the four re-expressed variables", y = "Rank of residual D²") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 6: Rank of each named bird’s residual D² among all 333 penguins (1 = most unusual), as the model grows. The first column ignores species, using the same four re-expressed variables, so its ranks differ a little from the book’s D² on the raw measures. The rank axis is on a log scale.





Three birds don’t care how they are compared. Once species is in the model, Cyrano, Snub Nose and the BFG hold the top three places, whatever else is added. Their oddities are in the shape of the bill and the build of the body, and nothing about their sex or the year they were measured explains them away. Tinkerbell rises when she is compared with other females: she is small even for a female Chinstrap. Average Joe stays ordinary throughout.
Falstaff is the exception. With species alone, he ranks 9th. Compared with Adélie males, the one group in which males are stouter than females, and with birds measured in 2007, the year of short flippers, he drops to 34th. He is still the stoutest bird of all on the raw ratio \(M / F^3\), and still well out in the tail on stoutness, so I’ll keep his name. But part of his stoutness is explained by who he is and when he was measured. That depends on a judgment: adjusting for year treats the 2007 flippers as a measurement artifact. If the difference were real, Falstaff would deserve his rank in the species model. Every term added to a model is a decision about what counts as unremarkable.
The fuller model also turns up new candidates for names. Gentoo male 179, measured in 2007, ranks 4th, and three Adélie females from 2009 (cases 137, 109 and 117) enter the top eight. They have names waiting for them too.
This is also where the post meets the book again. In Chapter 14, a robust multivariate linear model, heplots::robmlm(), down-weights the cases with large residuals. Its four lowest weights go to Cyrano, Snub Nose, the BFG and Gentoo 179: much the same birds, found by a different route. A robust fit of the model here does the same, giving Cyrano a weight of 0 and Snub Nose 0.05, while Falstaff keeps 0.81.







NoteAbout the banner





The banner image was made by ChatGPT, not drawn from the data. I asked it to read an earlier draft of this post, with Table 1, and to design a banner of the six birds: in sunglasses, in my species colors, and with sizes, shapes and bills that reflect their measurements. It took five rounds: tinting the bellies so the species could be told apart at thumbnail size, making Cyrano’s bill longer, adding the sashes with their names, and finally renaming Snub Nose and cutting Average Joe down to size.
It’s a caricature, and an instructive one. Cyrano’s bill was doubled on purpose, to make the point at banner size. Average Joe was a different matter. The prompt described him, correctly, as having “the largest overall frame” of the six, as a Gentoo male should, and the image generator read “largest” as “much the largest”: he stood half again as tall as Tinkerbell. In the data, he is only about 20% bigger in each linear dimension than she is (taking \(\sqrt{F \times M^{1/3}}\), a length-like version of body size, as the measure), and about 12% bigger than Falstaff. In fact, all six are within about 20% of each other. Shrunk by about 10%, he is still a little large, but closer to the truth. Which makes, in its way, the point of the post: Average Joe is average for a Gentoo, and how unusual a bird looks depends on what you compare it with.

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Further reading
The earlier posts in this series

Thinking about Penguin Variables: bill size and shape as an alternative view of bill length and depth.
Penguin Bodies: Size and Stoutness: the same idea for flipper length and body mass.

Naming and labeling points

Thompson, C. (2022). Level Up Your Labels: Tips and Tricks for Annotating Plots. Poster, useR! 2022. https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/
Friendly, M. (in preparation). Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Online at https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/. Cyrano and her companions first appear in Chapter 4, and come back in the chapter on influence and robust estimation for multivariate models.
Friendly, M., Fox, J., & Monette, G. heplots: Visualizing Tests in Multivariate Linear Models. R package. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=heplots. See noteworthy().
Fox, J., & Weisberg, S. (2018). An R Companion to Applied Regression (3rd ed.). Sage. The car package, whose id argument labels unusual points in nearly every plot.

The data

Gorman, K. B., Williams, T. D., & Fraser, W. R. (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus Pygoscelis). PLoS ONE, 9(3), e90081. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0090081
Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. R package version 0.1.0. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218

The namesakes

Edmond Rostand, Cyrano de Bergerac (1897). The nose speech is in Act I, scene 4.
Xenophon, Symposium, chapter 5: Socrates’ beauty contest with Critobulus, nose included.
William Shakespeare, Henry IV, Part 1 (c. 1597), for Falstaff.
J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), for Tinker Bell.
Roald Dahl, The BFG (1982).

title: Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”
text:
Footnotes


My consultant on this point, Big Bird of Sesame Street, agreed with the plan, but cautioned that at 8 feet 2 inches he has never once been called stout. By my measures, he’d be the BFG of Sesame Street.↩︎

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Data analysis usually starts with the variables as they were recorded. But the way a variable was measured is not necessarily the way it is best thought about:

A researcher records height and weight because those are easy to measure. But a physician may care more about body mass index, an expression of weight relative to height.
A chemist records concentrations of compounds, but the meaningful quantities may be their ratios.
Two raters assess a collection of patients on several measures of outcome in therapy, but our main interest might be in how these agree or disagree.

The Palmer penguins data (Gorman, Williams & Fraser, 2014) have recently become a familiar example in multivariate analysis. Penguins of three species on islands near Palmer Station in Antarctica were measured on four aspects of their bodies. Two of the variables, bill_length and bill_depth, describe the penguin’s bill (technically, the culmen, the upper ridge of the bill): its length from the base to the tip, and its depth, top to bottom, at the base (Figure 1).






Figure 1: The two bill measurements: length, from the base of the bill to its tip, and depth, top to bottom at the base. Artwork by Allison Horst.



Plotted against each other, they produce one of the best known examples of Simpson’s paradox (Figure 2): within each species, longer bills are deeper, but across the species, the relation is negative. But maybe, there’s a simple re-framing of the variables recorded into ones better thought about, that makes Simpson disappear.






Figure 2: Simpson’s paradox in the penguin bills. Left: ignoring species, longer bills are shallower. Middle: by species, the relation is positive for each. Right: shifting each species to the grand means shows the within-species relations, with differences in slopes and covariances.



This post asks a simple question: what do these two measurements really represent for penguins? Length and depth are not biologically two separate traits of a bill; together they describe one object: its beak. Two natural questions about any such object are:

How big is it? — its size
What proportions does it have? — its shape: is it long and slender, or short and stubby?

This suggests replacing (length, depth) with:
\[
\text{Size} = L \times D \qquad \text{Shape} = L / D \; ,
\]
or, more conveniently, their logarithms which are additive rather than multiplicative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log \text{Size}  &= \log L + \log D \\
\log \text{Shape} &= \log L - \log D \; .
\end{aligned}
\]
The units matter here: Size is (proportional to) the area of the bill’s profile, is in mm2; but shape is a dimensionless ratio, about 2 for a bill twice as long as it is deep. That’s easy to think about!
The size and shape idea goes back to the early days of multivariate morphometrics (Jolicoeur & Mosimann, 1960; Mosimann, 1970), where the first principal component of log measurements was often interpreted as “size” and the remaining ones as “shape”. Here we take a simpler, more direct route, defining size and shape from what the variables mean, and then asking whether the data agree in these two different representations.


In matrix terms, the log size–shape variables are a linear transformation of the log length–depth variables,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \log \text{Size} \\ \log \text{Shape} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \phantom{-}1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \log L \\ \log D \end{pmatrix}
= \mathbf{T} \begin{pmatrix} \log L \\ \log D \end{pmatrix} \; .
\]
The columns of \(\mathbf{T}\) are orthogonal and of equal length (\(\sqrt{2}\)), so \(\mathbf{T}\) is just a rotation by 45° (and a rescaling by \(\sqrt{2}\)). Nothing about the data has changed; we are simply looking at the same point cloud from a different angle. Consequently:

Every multivariate test (MANOVA, Hotelling’s \(T^2\), canonical discriminant analysis) gives identical results in the two coordinate systems, because these are invariant under nonsingular linear transformations of the responses.
Univariate analyses, and plots, are not invariant. They depend on which directions we choose as our axes.

The payoff, if there is one, is in interpretation: in the right coordinates, the story may be simpler.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Data and setup
The data used here is heplots::peng, a cleaned version of palmerpenguins::penguins (Gorman, Williams & Fraser, 2014) with the 333 complete cases and shorter variable names. Load the data and calculate the new size and shape variables.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(car)
library(heplots)

data(peng, package = "heplots")

peng <- peng |>
  mutate(
    size       = bill_length * bill_depth,
    shape      = bill_length / bill_depth,
    log_length = log(bill_length),
    log_depth  = log(bill_depth),
    log_size   = log_length + log_depth,
    log_shape  = log_length - log_depth,
    log_mass   = log(body_mass)
  )


Throughout, the species are shown in the colors of Allison Horst’s penguin artwork: orange for Adelie, purple for Chinstrap, green for Gentoo.


Code
peng_cols <- c(Adelie = "#F37A00", Chinstrap = "#6A3D9A", Gentoo = "#33a02c")

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))
scale_penguins <- list(
  scale_color_manual(values = peng_cols, aesthetics = c("colour", "fill"))
)


Rather than legends, the plots label the species directly. Two small helpers do the work: species_labels() places a label at each species’ mean, and peng_plot() draws a scatterplot with points, 68% and 95% data ellipses, the within-species regression lines and (optionally) the dashed regression line for all penguins pooled, ignoring species.


Code
species_labels <- function(x, y, data = peng, by = NULL, size = 5) {
  means <- data |>
    group_by(species, across(all_of(by))) |>
    summarise(x = mean({{ x }}), y = mean({{ y }}), .groups = "drop")
  geom_label(data = means, aes(x = x, y = y, label = species, color = species),
             fill = "white", alpha = 0.75, size = size, fontface = "bold",
             inherit.aes = FALSE)
}

peng_plot <- function(x, y, data = peng, pooled = TRUE, by = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = {{ x }}, y = {{ y }},
                        color = species, shape = species, fill = species)) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
    stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.68, alpha = 0.15) +
    stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.95, alpha = 0.10) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
    scale_penguins +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  if (pooled)
    p <- p + geom_smooth(aes(x = {{ x }}, y = {{ y }}), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                         method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
                         se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed",
                         linewidth = 1)
  p + species_labels({{ x }}, {{ y }}, data = data, by = by)
}

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
section: Two views of the same beaks
text:
Two views of the same beaks
Figure 3 shows the familiar view on the left and the size–shape view on the right.


Code
p1 <- peng_plot(bill_length, bill_depth) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", title = "Length & depth")

p2 <- peng_plot(log_size, log_shape) +
  labs(x = "log Size = log(L x D)", y = "log Shape = log(L / D)",
       title = "Size & shape")

p1 + p2








Figure 3: Left: bill depth vs. bill length, showing Simpson’s paradox: positive slopes within species, a negative slope (dashed) overall. Right: the same data as log shape vs. log size. The species now differ mainly in the vertical direction, and size and shape are nearly unrelated within each species.





Several things change in the size–shape view:

The paradox disappears. The within-species regression lines are nearly flat and the pooled line is nearly flat too. There is no longer a conflict between the within-group and between-group relations to explain.
The ellipses are nearly circular and their axes are roughly parallel to the coordinate axes. Within a species, size and shape vary nearly independently.
The species separate along one axis. Shape alone distinguishes all three species: Adelie have the stubbiest bills, Gentoo the most slender, with Chinstrap in between. Size adds a second, smaller distinction: Chinstrap bills are larger than those of the other two.

The species means tell the same story in natural units. Chinstrap bills are about 25% larger than the other species. A Gentoo bill is, on average, over three times as long as it is deep; an Adelie bill only about twice. That’s the relationship between the measured variable that makes the means appear in a triangular shape in (\(L, D\))-space with correlated variables, and shows the pattern we observed in (\(\text{Size}, \text{Shape}\))-space, where there is no correlation within-species and the interpretation is simpler.


Code
peng |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            length = mean(bill_length), depth = mean(bill_depth),
            size = mean(size), shape = mean(shape))


#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   species       n length depth  size shape
#>   <fct>     <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie      146   38.8  18.3  714.  2.12
#> 2 Chinstrap    68   48.8  18.4  902.  2.65
#> 3 Gentoo      119   47.6  15.0  715.  3.18

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Seeing the rotation
Because the size–shape coordinates are a 45\(^o\) rotation of the log length–depth coordinates, we can draw them directly on a plot of the logs. In Figure 4 the solid gray lines connect bills of the same size \((\log L + \log D = \text{constant})\) and the dashed lines connect bills of the same shape \((\log L - \log D = \text{constant})\). The lines are drawn at round values of \(L \times D\) (in steps of 100 mm2) and of \(L / D\) (in steps of 0.5), a few of which are labeled. With an aspect ratio of 1, the two sets of lines meet at right angles.


Show the code
iso_size  <- tibble(size  = seq(400, 1200, by = 100), k = log(size))
iso_shape <- tibble(shape = seq(1.5, 4, by = 0.5),   k = log(shape))

# label a couple of lines of each kind, in empty space
lab_size  <- iso_size  |> filter(size %in% c(800, 1000)) |>
  mutate(y = 3.06, x = k - y, label = paste0("L x D = ", size))
lab_shape <- iso_shape |> filter(shape %in% c(2.5, 3)) |>
  mutate(y = c(2.60, 2.55), x = k + y, label = paste0("L / D = ", shape))

peng_plot(log_length, log_depth, pooled = FALSE) +
  geom_abline(data = iso_size, aes(intercept = k, slope = -1),
              color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(data = iso_shape, aes(intercept = -k, slope = 1),
              color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_label(data = lab_size, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), angle = -45,
             size = 3.5, color = "gray30", fill = "white", linewidth = 0,
             inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_label(data = lab_shape, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), angle = 45,
             size = 3.5, color = "gray30", fill = "white", linewidth = 0,
             inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(3.44, 4.12), ylim = c(2.50, 3.10), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "log Bill length", y = "log Bill depth")








Figure 4: Log bill depth vs. log bill length, with lines of constant size (solid gray, slope -1) and constant shape (dashed, slope +1). The within-species ellipses are elongated along the size direction; the species are separated along the shape direction.





Read this way, the Simpson’s paradox in the original plot has a simple explanation. Within a species, bills vary mostly in size: big birds have bills that are both longer and deeper, so the within-species slopes are positive. Between species, the main difference is in shape: going from Adelie to Gentoo, bills get longer but shallower, so the between-species relation is negative.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Do the data agree?
I chose size and shape on substantive grounds, not from the data. Two quick checks show the choice is well supported, in that there is a natural translation of statistical ideas from (L, D) space to (Size, Shape) space.
Within-species correlations. If size and shape are natural dimensions for variation within a species, they should be close to uncorrelated there.


Code
within_r <- function(x, y)
  peng |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(r = cor({{ x }}, {{ y }})) |>
    bind_rows(tibble(species = "(pooled)",
                     r = cor(pull(peng, {{ x }}), pull(peng, {{ y }}))))

full_join(within_r(bill_length, bill_depth) |> rename(r_length_depth = r),
          within_r(log_size, log_shape)     |> rename(r_size_shape = r),
          by = "species")


#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   species   r_length_depth r_size_shape
#>   <chr>              <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie             0.386       0.0398
#> 2 Chinstrap          0.654       0.144 
#> 3 Gentoo             0.654      -0.0188
#> 4 (pooled)          -0.229       0.0727


The within-species correlations of length and depth are moderate to large, and differ in sign from the pooled correlation. Those of size and shape are all quite small.
Within-species principal components. The first principal component of the within-species covariance matrix of (log L, log D) is the direction of greatest variation within a species. If this is “size”, it should point at 45°, along the vector \((1, 1)/\sqrt{2}\).


Code
peng |>
  group_by(species) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    e <- eigen(cov(cbind(.x$log_length, .x$log_depth)))
    v <- e$vectors[, 1] * sign(e$vectors[1, 1])
    tibble(PC1_length = v[1], PC1_depth = v[2],
           pct_var = 100 * e$values[1] / sum(e$values),
           angle   = atan2(v[2], v[1]) * 180 / pi)
  })


#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#> # Groups:   species [3]
#>   species   PC1_length PC1_depth pct_var angle
#>   <fct>          <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie         0.739     0.673    69.7  42.3
#> 2 Chinstrap      0.763     0.647    83.2  40.3
#> 3 Gentoo         0.699     0.715    82.8  45.6


For each species the first component lies within a few degrees of 45° and accounts for 70–83% of the within-species variance. The dominant direction of variation within each species is, almost exactly, size.
Figure 5 shows this directly. Each species has been shifted to its own means, which removes the differences between species (mostly in shape) and leaves only the variation within species. Each species’ first principal component axis is drawn through the origin, ±2 standard deviations long, against the size direction (slope +1, dashed, as in Figure 4) and the perpendicular shape direction (slope −1, solid).


Show the code
peng_c <- peng |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(c_length = log_length - mean(log_length),
         c_depth  = log_depth  - mean(log_depth)) |>
  ungroup()

pc1 <- peng_c |>
  group_by(species) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    e <- eigen(cov(cbind(.x$c_length, .x$c_depth)))
    v <- e$vectors[, 1] * sign(e$vectors[1, 1])
    r <- 2 * sqrt(e$values[1])
    tibble(x = -r * v[1], y = -r * v[2], xend = r * v[1], yend = r * v[2],
           angle = atan2(v[2], v[1]) * 180 / pi)
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s: %.0f°", species, angle),
         # the PC1 axes nearly coincide, so stack their labels on the right
         lab_x = 0.15, lab_y = -0.04 - 0.035 * (row_number() - 1))

ggplot(peng_c, aes(x = c_length, y = c_depth, color = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_abline(slope =  1, intercept = 0, color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(slope = -1, intercept = 0, color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.15, y = -0.15, label = "size direction", angle = 45,
           vjust = -0.5, color = "gray30", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.13, y = 0.13, label = "shape direction", angle = -45,
           vjust = -0.5, color = "gray30", size = 4.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.68, alpha = 0.05, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = pc1, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               linewidth = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE,
               color = peng_cols[as.character(pc1$species)]) +
  geom_label(data = pc1, aes(x = lab_x, y = lab_y, label = label, color = species),
             fill = "white", size = 4.5, fontface = "bold",
             hjust = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = -0.04 + 0.035, label = "PC1 angle",
           hjust = 0, color = "gray30", size = 4.5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.2, 0.25), ylim = c(-0.2, 0.2)) +
  scale_penguins +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "log Bill length (centered within species)",
       y = "log Bill depth (centered within species)")








Figure 5: Within-species variation in log bill length and depth, with each species centered at its means. Ellipses are 68% data ellipses; the thick lines are each species’ first principal component axis. All three lie close to the size direction (dashed). The Adelie ellipse is the least elongated, so its first component is less dominant.





Two features of the plot carry the argument. First, the three first component axes very nearly coincide with each other and with the size diagonal: the species share a common pattern of within-species variation, and that pattern is variation in size. Second, the ellipses are elongated along this diagonal and shorter across it: within a species, penguins differ much more in how big their bills are than in their proportions. The Adelie ellipse is the roundest of the three, which matches its smaller share of variance on the first component (70%, against about 83% for the other two).
This is also why the size and shape coordinates make the within-species correlations vanish. Rotating the coordinate axes to lie (nearly) along the long and short axes of these ellipses is what makes the two new variables nearly uncorrelated.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
One variable at a time
A multivariate view is not always on authors’ minds. Some readers of a paper, on multivariate data like the penguins, may only be shown tables or plots for one variable at a time. Here the size–shape representation does even better, because it concentrates the species differences in a single variable (Figure 6).


Show the code
peng_long <- peng |>
  select(species, bill_length, bill_depth, log_size, log_shape) |>
  pivot_longer(-species, names_to = "variable") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable,
                           levels = c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "log_size", "log_shape")))

dens_peaks <- peng_long |>
  group_by(variable, species) |>
  summarise(d = list(density(value)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(x = sapply(d, \(d) d$x[which.max(d$y)]),
         y = sapply(d, \(d) max(d$y)))

ggplot(peng_long, aes(x = value, fill = species, color = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_label(data = dens_peaks, aes(x = x, y = y, label = species, color = species),
             fill = "white", alpha = 0.75, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold",
             vjust = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  scale_penguins +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 6: Densities of the four bill variables by species. Neither bill length nor bill depth separates all three species; log shape does, with little overlap.





The proportion of variance accounted for by species, \(\eta^2\), in a one-way ANOVA of each variable puts numbers on this:


Code
eta2 <- function(v) {
  a <- anova(lm(reformulate("species", v), data = peng))
  a[1, "Sum Sq"] / sum(a[, "Sum Sq"])
}
sapply(c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "log_size", "log_shape"), eta2)


#> bill_length  bill_depth    log_size   log_shape 
#>      0.7066      0.6764      0.3986      0.8900


Shape accounts for nearly 90% of the variance; neither length nor depth reaches 75%.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Sex differences: bigger, not different
Male penguins are larger than females. Does this extend to the shape of their bills? Figure 7 suggests not.


Code
peng_plot(log_size, log_shape, pooled = FALSE, by = "sex") +
  facet_wrap(~ sex, labeller = as_labeller(c(f = "Female", m = "Male"))) +
  labs(x = "log Size", y = "log Shape")








Figure 7: Log size and log shape by species, separately for females and males. The configuration of the species is the same in both panels, but shifted to the right for males: males have larger bills of the same shape.





A two-way MANOVA model confirms this. As promised, the multivariate tests are the same whichever pair of variables we use:


Code
mod_LD <- lm(cbind(log_length, log_depth) ~ species + sex, data = peng)
mod_SS <- lm(cbind(log_size, log_shape)   ~ species + sex, data = peng)

Anova(mod_LD)


#> 
#> Type II MANOVA Tests: Pillai test statistic
#>         Df test stat approx F num Df den Df Pr(>F)    
#> species  2     1.491      482      4    658 <2e-16 ***
#> sex      1     0.562      210      2    328 <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
Anova(mod_SS)


#> 
#> Type II MANOVA Tests: Pillai test statistic
#>         Df test stat approx F num Df den Df Pr(>F)    
#> species  2     1.491      482      4    658 <2e-16 ***
#> sex      1     0.562      210      2    328 <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


But the univariate tests now separate the two effects cleanly. Species differ strongly in both size and shape; the sexes differ strongly in size and not at all in shape.


Code
summary(aov(mod_SS))


#>  Response log_size :
#>              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
#> species       2   2.94   1.467     246 <2e-16 ***
#> sex           1   2.47   2.470     415 <2e-16 ***
#> Residuals   329   1.96   0.006                   
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>  Response log_shape :
#>              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
#> species       2  10.85    5.43 1333.21 <2e-16 ***
#> sex           1   0.00    0.00    0.42   0.52    
#> Residuals   329   1.34    0.00                   
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


In the original variables, the sex effect is spread over both length and depth, and the reader has to work out that the two increases are in proportion.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
HE plots
Hypothesis–error (HE) plots show these models directly. In each panel of Figure 8, the E ellipse shows the within-group (residual) covariance, and the H ellipses show the variation of the species means and the sex means, scaled here so that their size is comparable to the error ellipse (size = "effect").


Code
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1) + 0.1)
heplot(mod_LD, size = "effect", fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, asp = 1,
       xlab = "log Bill length", ylab = "log Bill depth")
heplot(mod_SS, size = "effect", fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, asp = 1,
       xlab = "log Size", ylab = "log Shape")
par(op)








Figure 8: HE plots for the MANOVA of bill measures on species and sex. Left: log length and log depth. Right: log size and log shape. The two plots are the same picture rotated by 45 degrees. In the right panel, the sex effect is a horizontal line (size only) and the error ellipse is aligned with the axes.





In the size–shape version:

The error ellipse has its axes parallel to the coordinate axes: residual size and shape are uncorrelated.
The sex effect degenerates to a line (one degree of freedom) that is almost exactly horizontal: a pure size difference.
The species ellipse is tall and narrow: species differ mostly in shape, with Chinstrap displaced to the right by its larger bills.

The within-species data ellipses (Figure 9) show the same alignment, with the pooled within-group ellipse in black.


Code
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1) + 0.1)
cols <- c(peng_cols, "black")
covEllipses(cbind(log_length, log_depth) ~ species, data = peng,
            pooled = TRUE, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, col = cols,
            xlab = "log Bill length", ylab = "log Bill depth", asp = 1)
covEllipses(cbind(log_size, log_shape) ~ species, data = peng,
            pooled = TRUE, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, col = cols,
            xlab = "log Size", ylab = "log Shape", asp = 1)
par(op)








Figure 9: Within-species 68% data ellipses and the pooled within-group ellipse (black), in log length–depth coordinates (left) and log size–shape coordinates (right).

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Size, shape, and body mass
Thinking of bill size as an area suggests one more question. If bills simply scaled with the rest of the body (isometric growth), bill area would grow as body mass to the 2/3 power, since mass is proportional to volume. On log scales, this means a slope of 2/3 for log size on log mass, and a slope of 0 for log shape (Figure 10).


Code
p3 <- peng_plot(log_mass, log_size) +
  labs(x = "log Body mass", y = "log Bill size")
p4 <- peng_plot(log_mass, log_shape) +
  labs(x = "log Body mass", y = "log Bill shape")
p3 + p4








Figure 10: Bill size (left) and bill shape (right) vs. body mass, on log scales. Bill size increases with body mass within each species; bill shape does not depend on body mass within any species, although the pooled line (dashed) suggests that it does.





The within-species slopes are:


Code
slopes <- function(y) {
  b <- coef(lm(reformulate("species / log_mass - 1", y), data = peng))
  b[grep(":log_mass", names(b))]
}
rbind(log_size = slopes("log_size"), log_shape = slopes("log_shape")) |>
  `colnames<-`(levels(peng$species))


#>             Adelie Chinstrap   Gentoo
#> log_size   0.61816   0.70792  0.91315
#> log_shape -0.01608  -0.01493 -0.04532


Shape is unrelated to body mass within all three species. The positive pooled slope in the right panel is another between-species effect, not a within-species one: Gentoo are both the heaviest penguins and the ones with the most slender bills. The size slopes for Adelie and Chinstrap are close to the isometric value of 2/3; Gentoo bills grow faster than isometry would predict. These are rough, descriptive slopes (mass and bill measures both contain measurement error, so ordinary least squares slopes are attenuated), but they illustrate that thinking about what a variable measures can suggest a baseline to compare against, here the value 2/3, that the raw variables would not.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
section: Sums and differences: the Tukey trick
text:
Sums and differences: the Tukey trick
Here’s a trick I learned from John Tukey. When two variables \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are commensurable, measured in the same units and on comparable scales, and are positively correlated, you can always replace them by their sum (or mean) and their difference without losing information, and often with a gain in interpretability:
\[
s = x_1 + x_2 \qquad d = x_1 - x_2 \; .
\]
This is the same 45° rotation used above for size and shape. As a graphical method, the plot of the difference \(d\) against the mean \(s/2\) is known as the Tukey mean-difference plot (Cleveland, 1993, pp. 22–23). In medicine, where it is the standard way to compare two methods of measuring the same quantity, it is called the Bland–Altman plot (Bland & Altman, 1986); see the Wikipedia article for a description and variants.
As we did for the penguins, that article recommends taking logs first when the two measurements differ by a ratio rather than an amount. Stated more directly, the diagram of penguin bills (Figure 1), suggested that the product, \(L \times D = \text{area}\) was a natural measure of bill size, while the ratio \(L / D\) could be interpreted as shape.
Two things make the Tukey trick work:

First, the new variables are nearly uncorrelated. The covariance of the sum and the difference is

\[
\text{Cov}(s, d) = \text{Var}(x_1) - \text{Var}(x_2) \; ,
\]
whatever the correlation between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). When the two variables have about the same variance, \(s\) and \(d\) are almost uncorrelated, no matter how strongly \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are correlated. If both have variance \(\sigma^2\), the variances of the sum and difference are \(2\sigma^2 (1 + r)\) and \(2\sigma^2 (1 - r)\), which shows where the variation went: the larger the correlation \(r\), the more of it is carried by the sum and the less by the difference.

Second, sums and differences usually mean something. The sum (or average) is the overall level or amount the two variables share; the difference is the contrast between them. For the penguins, these are size and shape. For two test scores, they are overall ability and a profile difference; for two measurement methods, they are the average reading and the disagreement between methods.

“Commensurable” is doing real work here. On the raw scale, bill length has two to three times the standard deviation of bill depth, so their sum and difference would still be correlated. On the log scale, each standard deviation is roughly a coefficient of variation, a relative spread, and these are nearly equal:


Code
peng |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(sd_length     = sd(bill_length),
            sd_depth      = sd(bill_depth),
            sd_log_length = sd(log_length),
            sd_log_depth  = sd(log_depth),
            r_size_shape  = cor(log_size, log_shape))


#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   species   sd_length sd_depth sd_log_length sd_log_depth r_size_shape
#>   <fct>         <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie         2.66    1.22         0.0686       0.0661       0.0398
#> 2 Chinstrap      3.34    1.14         0.0690       0.0618       0.144 
#> 3 Gentoo         3.11    0.986        0.0644       0.0654      -0.0188


Taking logs is what makes length and depth commensurable, and that, in turn, is why log size and log shape are so nearly uncorrelated within each species.
The same trick is a simple cure for collinearity among predictors in a regression. If \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are highly correlated, their separate coefficients are poorly determined; replacing them by \(s\) and \(d\) gives nearly uncorrelated predictors and an equivalent model. The coefficients are just re-expressed, as the average and the half-difference of the original ones:
\[
b_s = (b_1 + b_2) / 2 \qquad b_d = (b_1 - b_2) / 2 \; .
\]
For example, predicting log body mass from the log bill measurements (and species):


Code
m_LD <- lm(log_mass ~ species + log_length + log_depth, data = peng)
m_SS <- lm(log_mass ~ species + log_size   + log_shape, data = peng)
b <- coef(m_LD)[c("log_length", "log_depth")]
cbind(from_LD = c(log_size  = mean(b), log_shape = unname(-diff(b)) / 2),
      m_SS    = coef(m_SS)[c("log_size", "log_shape")])


#>           from_LD    m_SS
#> log_size   0.6641  0.6641
#> log_shape -0.1215 -0.1215


This doesn’t create information that wasn’t in the data. When \(r\) is large, the difference has little variance, and its coefficient is still estimated imprecisely. What the rotation does is put that imprecision where it belongs, in one interpretable contrast, rather than spreading it over both of the original coefficients.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
text:
Lessons

Look at what the variables mean before you analyze them. Length and depth are two measurements of one object. Re-expressing them as size and shape is a choice made on substantive grounds, not by fitting the data.
Equivalent models can tell different stories. Because the transformation is linear (in the logs) and nonsingular, nothing in the multivariate model changes: the fitted values, residuals and tests are the same. What changes is which questions are easy to answer and which plots are easy to read.
A good re-expression simplifies. In the size–shape coordinates, within-species variation is nearly uncorrelated, species differences are concentrated in one variable, the sex effect is confined to the other, and Simpson’s paradox goes away.
Check the choice against the data. Here the within-species principal components point almost exactly in the size direction, so the substantive choice and the empirical one agree.
Sums and differences are a general tool. For positively correlated, commensurable variables, rotating to their sum and difference gives nearly uncorrelated variables that are usually easier to interpret, and is a simple remedy for collinearity.

The same reasoning applies to the other penguin variables. Flipper length and body mass are also, in part, measures of overall size; one might go on to define an overall body size (for example, the mean of the four log measurements) and express each variable relative to it. That is a story for another post.
Update: That story is told in Penguin Bodies: Size and Stoutness. The series continues with Palmer Penguins Cry Out: “Call Me by My Name”, which uses bill shape and stoutness to find out what makes six named penguins unusual.
Note: This question was also explored by Fil (@fil) in the Observable notebook Penguin bills by shape.

title: Thinking about Penguin Variables
